title: Find All Duplicates in an Array
notes:
Task and constraints: Find all values that occur twice in nums, where length n and values are in [1,n]; use constant extra space apart from output.
Idea: For each x, compute i=abs(x)-1; if nums[i] is negative, append abs(x), otherwise negate nums[i] to mark that value's index.
Technique and why it applies: In-place sign marking uses array slots as visited flags, avoiding a separate set.
Invariant: After processing a prefix, a negative slot marks that its index's value has appeared at least once; later occurrences detect that sign.
Edge cases: Empty input returns []; [1,1] reports 1 on its second visit; distinct values produce no output. The method mutates nums and assumes every absolute value lies in 1..n.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space excluding output, because the loop visits each element once and uses only scalar variables.
complexity_reason: The loop makes one pass through n values, uses each absolute value as an index, and stores duplicates only in the output list.

title: Find All Duplicates in an Array
notes:
Task and constraints: Find duplicates in an int array of length n whose values are in [1,n], using sign marking instead of a set.
Idea: For each x, calculate i=Math.abs(x)-1; if nums[i] is negative, append abs(x), otherwise negate nums[i] as its seen marker.
Technique and why it applies: Index-based sign marking records whether a value appeared without allocating a membership structure.
Invariant: A negative slot marks a value whose index has been visited, so a later occurrence is recognized as a duplicate.
Edge cases: Empty input returns an empty list; [1,1] adds 1 once; distinct values add nothing. The input is modified. Math.abs(Integer.MIN_VALUE) overflows, but the problem's positive bounded values exclude that case.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space excluding output, since each array entry is visited once.
complexity_reason: The enhanced loop examines n values with constant work per value, and only the result list grows with the number of duplicates.

title: String Compression
notes:
Task and constraints: Compress chars in place by writing one character per run and decimal count digits only when the run exceeds one; return the written length.
Idea: read finds each run's end, write stores its character, and str(count) supplies count digits when count>1.
Technique and why it applies: Read/write pointers perform run-length encoding in place, with processed data overwritten only behind the read position.
Invariant: Before each outer iteration, chars[:write] contains the compressed encoding of all runs ending before read.
Edge cases: Empty input returns zero; ['a'] remains one character; twelve repeated characters become ['a','1','2']. The array is mutated, and the returned length marks the valid prefix.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space apart from a temporary count string, because each character is scanned and written a bounded number of times.
complexity_reason: The read pointer advances past each run once and the write pointer emits its character plus at most the run's count digits.

title: String Compression
notes:
Task and constraints: Compress a char array in place by encoding each run as its character and, when longer than one, the decimal count; return valid prefix length.
Idea: read scans equal characters through end, write records the run character, and Integer.toString(count) emits digits when needed.
Technique and why it applies: Two pointers perform run-length encoding without allocating a second result array.
Invariant: chars[0..write) is the correct compressed encoding of all runs preceding read.
Edge cases: An empty array returns zero; a single character needs no count; a run of twelve is written as its character followed by '1' and '2'. The array is mutated, and Java's conversion handles multi-digit counts.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space apart from a temporary digit string, because each input character belongs to one scanned run.
complexity_reason: The scans advance through chars once, while each run writes one character and at most its decimal count digits.

title: Add Two Numbers II
notes:
Task and constraints: Add two nonempty linked lists with digits in forward order and return a new linked list for the sum.
Idea: Copy each list's digits into a and b, pop least-significant digits, compute total with carry, and prepend each result digit to head.
Technique and why it applies: Stacks reverse access order so addition proceeds from least-significant digits without reversing input lists.
Invariant: After each addition, head contains the processed sum digits in forward order, and carry is the overflow for the next position.
Edge cases: Unequal lengths use zero when one stack empties; 7243+564 yields 7807; a final carry creates a leading node. Input lists are not rewired.
Complexity: O(m+n) time and O(m+n) auxiliary space for digit stacks and the output list.
complexity_reason: Both input lists are traversed once, each digit is popped at most once, and the stacks and output contain O(m+n) digits.

title: Add Two Numbers II
notes:
Task and constraints: Sum two nonempty forward-order digit lists and return a linked list containing the forward-order result.
Idea: a and b store digits in deques; pop from each nonempty deque, add carry, prepend sum%10, and update carry with integer division.
Technique and why it applies: Deques expose least-significant digits first while preserving the original lists' forward order.
Invariant: head stores the already processed suffix of the numeric sum, and carry is passed to the next more significant position.
Edge cases: Unequal lengths are handled by zero contributions from empty deques; 7243 plus 564 yields 7807; a final carry adds a leading node. Java int arithmetic suffices for two digits and carry under usual digit constraints.
Complexity: O(m+n) time and O(m+n) space for the two deques and result nodes.
complexity_reason: Each linked list is traversed once and every stored digit is popped once; the deques and newly allocated result use linear space.

title: Arithmetic Slices II - Subsequence
notes:
Task and constraints: Count arithmetic subsequences of length at least three; the DP groups partial sequences by ending index and common difference.
Idea: For each pair j<i, compute diff, read dp[j][diff], add that count to answer, and store count+1 in dp[i][diff] for extensions and the new pair.
Technique and why it applies: Difference-keyed dynamic programming counts sequences by final index and difference, extending every shorter arithmetic sequence.
Invariant: dp[i][d] counts subsequences of length at least two ending at i with difference d; only extensions of length at least two contribute to answer.
Edge cases: Fewer than three values returns zero; [2,4,6] contributes one triple; equal values use difference zero. Python integers avoid count overflow.
Complexity: O(n²) expected time and O(n²) space for pair transitions and per-index difference maps.
complexity_reason: The nested i,j loops inspect every index pair once, and the difference maps can hold O(n²) pair states.

title: Arithmetic Slices II - Subsequence
notes:
Task and constraints: Count arithmetic subsequences of length at least three, grouping partial sequences by ending index and difference.
Idea: For each i and earlier j, compute long d, add dp[j][d] to answer, and increase dp[i][d] by that count plus one for the pair.
Technique and why it applies: Dynamic programming by difference reuses counts of shorter arithmetic subsequences that can be extended with nums[i].
Invariant: Each dp[i] map stores counts of length-at-least-two subsequences ending at i; answer adds only prior sequences that become length at least three.
Edge cases: Arrays shorter than three yield zero; [2,4,6] contributes one; repeated numbers use difference zero. long prevents subtraction overflow, but answer is int and can overflow for very large counts.
Complexity: O(n²) expected time and O(n²) space because each pair updates one hash-map state.
complexity_reason: The nested loops process all n(n-1)/2 pairs, and each per-index map can retain states for many distinct differences.

title: Find All Numbers Disappeared in an Array
notes:
Task and constraints: Return values missing from [1,n] in an n-element array whose values all lie in [1,n], using in-place marking.
Idea: For each x, negate the entry at abs(x)-1; afterward, indices whose values remain positive identify missing values i+1.
Technique and why it applies: Sign marking turns the input array into a visited-index table without an extra membership array.
Invariant: After the marking pass, an index is negative exactly when its corresponding value appeared in nums.
Edge cases: Empty input returns []; [1,1] leaves index 1 positive so 2 is reported; a permutation of [1..n] produces no missing values. The input is mutated, and absolute values are used before indexing.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space excluding output, with two linear passes and scalar indexing.
complexity_reason: The marking loop handles n entries and the final comprehension scans all n slots to build the missing-value list.

title: Find All Numbers Disappeared in an Array
notes:
Task and constraints: Find values absent from [1,n] in an n-element int array whose values lie in [1,n].
Idea: The first loop uses abs(x)-1 to negate a corresponding slot; the second loop adds i+1 for each slot still positive.
Technique and why it applies: In-place sign marking encodes membership in array signs and avoids a separate boolean array.
Invariant: After marking, negative nums[i] means value i+1 occurred in the original array, while a positive slot means it did not.
Edge cases: Empty input returns an empty list; duplicates only re-negate an already negative slot; a complete permutation returns no missing values. The method mutates nums and relies on the stated positive range for Math.abs.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space excluding output, because two passes inspect at most n entries.
complexity_reason: One loop performs n index marks and the following loop checks each of n positions, storing only missing values in the output list.

title: Delete Node in a BST
notes:
Task and constraints: Delete the node with key from a BST and return the updated root while preserving BST ordering.
Idea: Recurse left or right by comparison; on a match return the sole child if one is absent, or copy the right-subtree minimum and delete that successor.
Technique and why it applies: BST-directed recursion searches one branch, and inorder-successor replacement preserves ordering when the target has two children.
Invariant: Each recursive call returns a valid BST containing the original subtree's keys except the requested key if present.
Edge cases: A null root stays null; deleting a leaf returns None to its parent; a two-child node takes the leftmost value in its right subtree. Recursion depth can reach O(h) for a skewed tree.
Complexity: O(h) time and O(h) call-stack space for tree height h, including successor search and recursive deletion.
complexity_reason: The search and successor walk each follow tree links for at most O(h) steps, and recursive frames use O(h) space.

title: Delete Node in a BST
notes:
Task and constraints: Remove key from a BST and return the subtree root after maintaining the BST property.
Idea: Compare key with root.val and recurse into one child; a matching node returns its only child, or copies the minimum of the right subtree and recursively removes that successor.
Technique and why it applies: BST ordering directs the search down one path, while successor replacement handles the two-child case without breaking sorted order.
Invariant: Every returned subtree remains ordered and excludes the deleted key when it existed in that subtree.
Edge cases: Null root returns null; deleting a one-child node returns that child directly; two-child deletion walks left from root.right to find the successor. Recursion depth may reach h, and Java stack depth can limit a skewed tree.
Complexity: O(h) time and O(h) call-stack space for tree height h.
complexity_reason: The key search and successor scan traverse paths of at most height h, with one recursive frame per search level.

title: Sort Characters By Frequency
notes:
Task and constraints: Return s with the same characters arranged in nonincreasing frequency order.
Idea: Counter(s) counts each character, most_common() orders character-count pairs, and join repeats each character n times.
Technique and why it applies: Frequency counting groups identical characters, then ordering groups by count avoids sorting every occurrence independently.
Invariant: Each pair from most_common contributes exactly the original count of its character, preserving the input's character multiset.
Edge cases: Empty s returns an empty string; one repeated character stays unchanged; tied frequencies may appear in Counter's tie order. The output length equals len(s).
Complexity: O(n + u log u) time and O(u+n) space, where u is distinct characters, for counting, sorting keys, and constructing output.
complexity_reason: Counter scans n characters, ordering u distinct characters costs O(u log u), and the joined result contains n characters.

title: Sort Characters By Frequency
notes:
Task and constraints: Rearrange s so characters appear in decreasing frequency while preserving all character counts.
Idea: Map c counts characters, keys contains distinct characters sorted by descending counts, and nested loops append each key its recorded number of times to out.
Technique and why it applies: A frequency map plus sorting distinct keys orders character groups without sorting all n positions individually.
Invariant: Before each key is processed, out contains complete groups for all previously sorted keys and preserves their multiplicities.
Edge cases: Empty input yields an empty string; a repeated character is appended count times; equal-frequency keys may have unspecified relative order because HashMap iteration order is unspecified. StringBuilder avoids repeated immutable-string concatenation.
Complexity: O(n + u log u) time and O(u+n) space for counting, sorting u keys, and building output.
complexity_reason: The count pass reads n characters, key sorting orders u distinct entries, and StringBuilder stores n output characters.

title: Minimum Number of Arrows to Burst Balloons
notes:
Task and constraints: Find the minimum arrows needed to intersect every balloon interval; an empty interval list needs zero arrows.
Idea: Sort points by ending coordinate, place the first arrow at the first finish, and add an arrow only when a later interval starts beyond end.
Technique and why it applies: Earliest-end greedy selection chooses an arrow location that covers as many upcoming intervals as possible.
Invariant: end is the latest arrow position, and every processed interval is covered by one of the arrows counted in arrows.
Edge cases: Empty input returns zero; intervals sharing an endpoint need one arrow because start==end is covered; disjoint intervals need another arrow. Sorting mutates points.
Complexity: O(n log n) time for sorting plus a linear scan, and O(1) extra scan space apart from sort implementation.
complexity_reason: The intervals are sorted once by end coordinate and then scanned once, with only the arrow count and current endpoint retained.

title: Minimum Number of Arrows to Burst Balloons
notes:
Task and constraints: Compute the minimum vertical arrows needed to intersect every balloon interval, returning zero for no balloons.
Idea: After sorting by end coordinate, end is the first interval's endpoint; each later interval starting after end increments arrows and moves the endpoint.
Technique and why it applies: Greedy placement at the earliest finishing endpoint maximizes intervals hit by each arrow.
Invariant: Every interval processed so far intersects an arrow already placed, and end is the position of the last arrow.
Edge cases: Empty points returns zero; intervals touching at end share an arrow because the condition is strict >; large int endpoints are compared after casting to long. Sorting changes input order.
Complexity: O(n log n) time for sorting and O(n) scan time, with O(1) explicit auxiliary variables.
complexity_reason: Sorting dominates run time, then the loop checks each remaining interval once and stores only a long endpoint and count.

title: Minimum Moves to Equal Array Elements
notes:
Task and constraints: Find moves to equalize nums when each move increments n-1 elements; this implementation assumes nums is nonempty.
Idea: Compute minimum m and sum each difference x-m; this is equivalent to accounting for relative gaps rather than simulating operations.
Technique and why it applies: An algebraic identity reduces repeated moves to differences from the minimum, avoiding simulation of individual moves.
Invariant: Each term x-m accounts for the gap above the minimum in the transformed operation model.
Edge cases: A single value returns zero; [1,2,3] returns 3; negative values work with min and subtraction. Empty input raises an error at min(nums).
Complexity: O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space, since min and sum each scan the array and retain scalar state.
complexity_reason: The min and sum operations each traverse nums once, and the method creates no collection proportional to n.

title: Minimum Moves to Equal Array Elements
notes:
Task and constraints: Return moves to equalize all values when one move increments n-1 elements; the implementation expects a nonempty array.
Idea: The first loop finds min, and the second accumulates each (long)x-min into total before casting the result to int.
Technique and why it applies: The operation-count identity replaces simulation with a sum of each element's difference from the minimum.
Invariant: After the second loop's prefix, total equals the sum of differences for every processed value.
Edge cases: One element returns zero; [1,2,3] returns 3; negative values are supported. Casting long total to int can overflow if the true answer exceeds int range, and empty input is outside constraints.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(1) extra space because two loops inspect the array and only primitive variables are stored.
complexity_reason: Two passes each visit n integers, while the method stores the minimum and running total in primitive variables.

title: 4Sum II
notes:
Task and constraints: Count tuples with one index from each of four arrays whose selected values sum to zero.
Idea: sums counts every a+b from nums1 and nums2; each c,d pair contributes the frequency of -(c+d) to the result.
Technique and why it applies: Pair-sum hashing reduces four nested loops to pair generation and lookups.
Invariant: sums[t] equals the number of index pairs from the first two arrays with sum t, so each lookup counts matching tuples for that c,d pair.
Edge cases: Any empty array yields zero; duplicate values contribute multiple index combinations; negative values are supported. Python integers avoid overflow in sums and answer.
Complexity: O(n1*n2+n3*n4) expected time and O(n1*n2) space for the pair-sum Counter.
complexity_reason: The first two arrays create n1*n2 pair counts, and the second pair of arrays performs n3*n4 expected-time hash lookups.

title: 4Sum II
notes:
Task and constraints: Count tuples with one element from each of four arrays whose values sum to zero.
Idea: The first nested loops count every a+b in count; the second pair of loops adds the frequency of -x-y to ans.
Technique and why it applies: Hashing sums from two arrays lets pairs from the other arrays find matching combinations without a four-dimensional search.
Invariant: Each map frequency records how many a,b index pairs have that sum, and each lookup contributes matching tuples for the current c,d pair.
Edge cases: Any empty input array results in zero; repeated sums preserve multiplicity. long ans reduces intermediate answer overflow, but the final int cast can overflow; pair arithmetic uses int and can overflow for unrestricted values.
Complexity: O(n1*n2+n3*n4) expected time and O(n1*n2) map space.
complexity_reason: The nested loops enumerate each pair from a,b once and each pair from c,d once, storing frequencies for at most n1*n2 sums.
